claim: The US FTC Care Labeling Rule allows a temporary (hangtag) care label for fully reversible garments provided the label says 'Wash or dryclean, any normal method'.
reasoning: The claim conflates two separate, independent exemptions in 16 CFR 423.8 (Care Labeling Rule "Exemptions"). Exemption 1: textile wearing apparel that is totally reversible AND has no pockets is exempt from the permanent care label requirement; care information must still be given to the consumer via a hang tag, package, or other conspicuous means (FTC "Clothes Captioning" guide; Cornell LII 16 CFR 423.8; AAFA FAQ). There is no requirement that this hang tag say "Wash or dryclean, any normal method" — it carries the product's actual care instructions — and the reversible exemption does not apply if the garment has pockets. Exemption 2 (separate): any product that can be washed, dried, bleached, ironed and drycleaned by the harshest available procedures may use a temporary label reading "Wash or dry clean, any normal method" instead of a permanent label, regardless of reversibility. AAFA explicitly describes these as separate exemptions. So the claim's conditional linkage (reversible → must say "any normal method") is wrong, and it omits the "no pockets" condition. Note: eCFR blocked automated fetch; Cornell LII summary and FTC/AAFA guidance were used instead. Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/423.8 ; https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/clothes-captioning-complying-care-labeling-rule ; https://www.aafaglobal.org/AAFA/Solutions_Pages/Labeling_Frequently_Asked_Individual_Questions/Are_there_any_exemptions_to_the_Care_Labeling_Rule_.aspx
corrected_claim: Under 16 CFR 423.8 of the US FTC Care Labeling Rule, a garment that is totally reversible and has no pockets is exempt from the permanent care label requirement, but its care instructions must still be provided to consumers on a hang tag, package, or other conspicuous place before purchase (the wording is the product's actual care instructions, not a fixed phrase). Separately, any garment that can withstand the harshest washing, drying, bleaching, ironing and drycleaning procedures may use a temporary (non-permanent) label reading "Wash or dry clean, any normal method" instead of a permanent label; this exemption is independent of reversibility. A reversible bucket hat with pockets would not qualify for the reversible exemption.

claim: A Lambda Function URL synchronous invocation is capped at 6 MB request payload in BUFFERED mode, so a 10 MB image upload cannot pass through it and must use a presigned S3 PUT.
reasoning: Verified against current AWS docs (2026-09). The Lambda quotas page (docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html) lists "Invocation payload (request and response): 6 MB each for request and response (synchronous); 200 MB for each streamed response (synchronous); 1 MB (asynchronous)". Function URLs invoke via the synchronous Invoke API in BUFFERED mode, so the 6 MB request cap applies. The response-streaming page confirms RESPONSE_STREAM only raises the *response* limit to 200 MB; there is no request streaming, so the 6 MB request cap holds in both invoke modes. The function URL invocation doc states binary bodies are base64-encoded into the event ("body ... If the content type of the request is binary, the body is base64-encoded"), which inflates them ~33%, so the effective raw binary ceiling is about 4.5 MB, well under 10 MB. Adversarial angles checked: (1) Could RESPONSE_STREAM mode accept larger requests? No, it only affects responses. (2) Is the quota adjustable? The quotas table says these function execution limits "can't be changed" except as noted, and payload is not noted. (3) Could multipart/chunked uploads bypass it? Lambda buffers the whole request into the event; no bypass. The only imprecision is "must use a presigned S3 PUT": presigned PUT is the standard recommendation, but alternatives (S3 presigned POST, S3 multipart upload, CloudFront/S3 Transfer Acceleration, or chunking the file into <4.5 MB pieces across multiple invocations) also exist; this is a strengthening of wording, not a factual error. Overall the claim is accurate and slightly understates the problem because of base64 inflation.

claim: Terraform 1.10 and later supports native S3 backend state locking via use_lockfile = true, so no DynamoDB table or permissions are required for state locking with Terraform 1.15.
reasoning: Verified against the official S3 backend docs (developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/s3) and multiple independent sources. Native S3 locking via `use_lockfile = true` was introduced in Terraform 1.10 (as an experimental/opt-in feature) and promoted to GA in 1.11, at which point `dynamodb_table`, `dynamodb_endpoint`, and `endpoints.dynamodb` were marked deprecated; the docs currently state "DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated and will be removed in a future minor version." Terraform 1.15 exists (released 2026-04-29; v1.15.1 is current) and still accepts `dynamodb_table` with a deprecation warning, but does not require it. Locking works by writing a `<key>.tflock` object with an S3 conditional PutObject (If-None-Match). Minor caveats that don't refute the claim: (1) in 1.10 specifically the feature was labeled experimental, GA came in 1.11; (2) while no DynamoDB permissions are needed, the IAM principal does need s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, and s3:DeleteObject on the `.tflock` key (the state object itself needs no DeleteObject); (3) bucket versioning is recommended. So for a fresh Terraform 1.15 deployment, an S3 bucket alone with `use_lockfile = true` is sufficient and is the recommended, non-deprecated configuration.

claim: Bucket hat finished inside head circumference should be S 56.0 / M 58.0 / L 60.0 cm (a 2 cm grade) with a +/-1.0 cm tolerance, consistent with EN 13402 head-girth bands S 54-56, M 56-58, L 58-60 cm.
reasoning: Partially refuted. The numeric spec (S 56 / M 58 / L 60 cm, 2 cm grade, +/-1.0 cm tolerance) is plausible and matches industry practice: multiple hat sizing guides publish S 54-56, M 56-58, L 58-60, XL 60-62 cm bands (bon-clic-bon-genre, Sungrubbies), bucket-hat OEM charts sit in the same neighbourhood (Yukaihe: S 55-56, M 57-58, L 59-60; Sumkcaps: S 54-55, M 56-57, L 58-59), hat sizes grade in 1 cm steps (Lock & Co.) so a 2 cm S/M/L grade is a common two-step grouping, and a cap tech-pack guide (Specter OS) states "typical tolerances for headwear are +/-0.5 cm on crown height and brim dimensions, +/-1 cm on head circumference". What is contradicted is the attribution to EN 13402: EN 13402 does not define S/M/L letter-code bands for headwear. Per the standard (Wikipedia summary of EN 13402-2/-3), headwear is designated solely by head girth in cm as the primary dimension; letter codes are only defined for some body garments, and the 2017 revision (BSI) moved letter sizes into a separate Annex A section that does not cover head girth. EN 13402-3 does contain head-girth tables (Table 11 men, Table 25 women, Table 41 children in the 2013 edition), and products such as helmets are labelled with a cm range (e.g. "head girth 56-60 cm"), but the actual table intervals could not be verified (the sample PDFs are encrypted/unreadable and previews were 403). The generic EN 13402 girth rule ("4 cm intervals, +/-2 cm") applies to body garments, not specifically head girth. So the S 54-56 / M 56-58 / L 58-60 bands are trade convention, not EN 13402 bands. A secondary caution (not a refutation): those bands are body-measurement ranges; a finished inside circumference equal to the top of the band gives zero ease for the largest head in the band, whereas bucket-hat guidance typically adds ~1-1.5 cm wearing ease ("two-finger rule"), so the generator should state whether 56/58/60 is body or finished-with-ease. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_European_standard_for_size_labelling_of_clothes ; https://knowledge.bsigroup.com/products/size-designation-of-clothes-size-labelling-based-on-body-measurements-and-intervals ; https://www.specter-os.com/blog/cap-tech-pack ; https://www.bon-clic-bon-genre.us/content-how-to-determine-your-hat-size_0.htm ; https://www.sungrubbies.com/blogs/news-articles/how-to-determine-your-hat-size ; https://www.yukaihe.com/bucket-hat-sizing-fit-guide ; https://sumkcaps.com/bucket-hats-size-guide/ ; https://www.lockhatters.com/pages/hat-sizing ; https://happyoff.com/blogs/news/bucket-hat-sizing-technical-guide
corrected_claim: Bucket hat finished inside head circumference of S 56.0 / M 58.0 / L 60.0 cm (2 cm grade) with a +/-1.0 cm tolerance is a reasonable industry-convention spec: it aligns with widely used trade hat-size bands (S 54-56, M 56-58, L 58-60, XL 60-62 cm) and typical headwear tech-pack tolerances (+/-1 cm on head circumference, +/-0.5 cm on crown/brim). These letter bands are trade convention, not EN 13402: EN 13402 designates headwear by head girth in centimetres only (a labelled cm range such as "56-60 cm") and defines no S/M/L bands for head girth. State explicitly whether 56/58/60 is the target body head girth or the finished inside circumference including wearing ease (typically +1 to 1.5 cm for soft bucket hats).

Partially refuted: the react-pdf half is overstated; the PDFKit and Playwright halves hold up.

Issue #2638 is literally titled "Arabic characters not working since bidi support was added" — so citing it as evidence of *no* bidi support is self-contradicting. #3007 ("arabic in react-pdf issue", closed as not planned) and the still-open #3406 (Apr 2026, Arabic ligatures dropped during textkit bidi reordering with mixed LTR runs) show the support is buggy/incomplete, not absent. Playwright/Chromium: Chromium's print-to-PDF path (Skia) runs full HarfBuzz shaping + ICU bidi and embeds @font-face fonts (subsetted) automatically; multiple independent guides (BrowserStack, pdf4.dev, Medium Spring Boot+Playwright RTL article, blog.hompus.nl) corroborate. No contradicting evidence; plausible and well-supported.
corrected_claim: @react-pdf/renderer added native BiDi/RTL support in Feb 2024 (PR #2600 closed issue #1571; `direction: 'rtl'` is a documented style prop), but it is unreliable — regressions and gaps remain (#2638 undefined-glyph errors after bidi landed, #3007 Arabic broken across newlines closed as not-planned, #3406 Arabic ligatures dropped in mixed LTR/RTL lines still open as of Apr 2026), and mixed-direction text commonly still needs RLM markers and manual row-reverse layouts.
